Is a vector a certain kind of sequence?

Source: R/seq-predicates.R
seq-predicates.Rd

These functions are deprecated because scrutiny no longer uses them: the sequence mappers record how far each value was moved, in diff_var. They may be removed in a future version.

Predicates for numeric vectors, or vectors coercible to numeric:

  • is_seq_linear(): do all consecutive elements differ by the same amount?

  • is_seq_ascending(), is_seq_descending(): is every difference positive, or negative?

  • is_seq_dispersed(): is x centered on from, with each pair of values equidistant from it?

By default (test_linear = TRUE), the last three also test for linearity.

Usage

is_seq_linear(x, tolerance = .Machine$double.eps^0.5)

is_seq_ascending(x, test_linear = TRUE, tolerance = .Machine$double.eps^0.5)

is_seq_descending(x, test_linear = TRUE, tolerance = .Machine$double.eps^0.5)

is_seq_dispersed(
  x,
  from,
  test_linear = TRUE,
  tolerance = .Machine$double.eps^0.5
)

Arguments

x

Numeric, character, or factor vector. Strings and factor labels count as numbers as determined by is_numeric_like(); any that are not make the result FALSE. A logical vector is accepted only if all its values are NA. Any other type, such as a list or a data frame, is an error.

tolerance

Numeric. Tolerance for comparing values. Default is about 1.5e-8, as in dplyr::near(). It is never finer than the rounding error of arithmetic on the values, so 0 allows that error only.

test_linear

Logical. Should linearity be tested as well? Default is TRUE. Not in is_seq_linear().

from

Numeric, character, or factor, like x. Only in is_seq_dispersed(). The value x should be centered on.

Value

Logical (length 1). If x contains NA:

  • NA if some values substituted for the NAs would make x the kind of sequence in question and others would not.

  • FALSE if none would, e.g., because x is too short for it (two values for is_seq_ascending() and is_seq_descending(), three for is_seq_dispersed()).

  • TRUE if all would, as any one or two values are linear.

A missing from is handled the same way.

See also

validate::is_linear_sequence(), which is more permissive with NA and supports date-times.

Examples

is_seq_linear(x = 3:7)
#> Warning: `is_seq_linear()` was deprecated in scrutiny 1.0.0.
#> ℹ It may be removed in a future version of scrutiny.
#> [1] TRUE
is_seq_linear(x = c(3:7, 9))
#> [1] FALSE

# The other predicates test for linearity by default:
is_seq_ascending(x = c(2, 7, 9))
#> Warning: `is_seq_ascending()` was deprecated in scrutiny 1.0.0.
#> ℹ It may be removed in a future version of scrutiny.
#> [1] FALSE
is_seq_ascending(x = c(2, 7, 9), test_linear = FALSE)
#> [1] TRUE

is_seq_descending(x = c(9, 7, 2))
#> Warning: `is_seq_descending()` was deprecated in scrutiny 1.0.0.
#> ℹ It may be removed in a future version of scrutiny.
#> [1] FALSE
is_seq_descending(x = c(9, 7, 2), test_linear = FALSE)
#> [1] TRUE

is_seq_dispersed(x = c(2, 3, 5, 7, 8), from = 5)
#> Warning: `is_seq_dispersed()` was deprecated in scrutiny 1.0.0.
#> ℹ It may be removed in a future version of scrutiny.
#> [1] FALSE
is_seq_dispersed(x = c(2, 3, 5, 7, 8), from = 5, test_linear = FALSE)
#> [1] TRUE

# These fail their own test regardless of linearity:
is_seq_ascending(x = c(1, 7, 4), test_linear = FALSE)
#> [1] FALSE
is_seq_descending(x = c(9, 15, 3), test_linear = FALSE)
#> [1] FALSE
is_seq_dispersed(1:10, from = 5, test_linear = FALSE)
#> [1] FALSE
